value.overview: The Ruddy Quail-Dove (Geotrygon montana) is a compact, shy dove of tropical forests in the Americas. It spends much of its time walking quietly on the forest floor, where its rounded body and short tail give it a quail-like appearance. The species occurs from the Caribbean and southern Florida as a rare visitor through Central America and into northern and central South America. It is usually detected by movement, soft calls, or brief flights rather than by prolonged open views.
value.classification: The Ruddy Quail-Dove belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae and the genus Geotrygon. It is one of several forest-floor quail-doves found in the Neotropics.
value.identification: This stout, short-tailed dove is about 21–28 cm long. Adults are mainly rich reddish or chestnut brown above, with paler buff or cinnamon-brown underparts. A pale buff or whitish stripe below the eye is an important field mark, although it can be subtle in poor light. Males are generally more strongly colored, while females tend to be duller and less distinctly patterned. It often walks with a deliberate, quail-like gait on the ground.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Quail-Dove ranges through the West Indies, Central America, and much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring mainly in lowland and foothill forests, especially in humid regions, but also locally in drier woodland and forest edges. It may use primary forest, secondary growth, dense scrub, shaded plantations, and other habitats with substantial ground cover. Costa Rican records extend from the lowlands into foothill zones, locally reaching approximately 1,200–1,400 m.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica and is not considered a regular long-distance migrant there. Local movements may occur in response to food availability, weather, or changes in habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information varies across its broad range. The species usually builds a loose, flimsy platform of twigs in low vegetation, although nests may sometimes be placed on the ground or on a low stump. Two buff-colored eggs are typically laid. In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported during the wetter part of the year, with observations concentrated in spring and early summer in some regions. Nest placement in dense cover helps conceal the adults and young from predators.
value.dietFeeding: The Ruddy Quail-Dove forages mainly on the ground, where it searches through leaf litter for fallen fruits, seeds, and other plant material. It may also take small invertebrates such as insects and worms. Individuals are often encountered alone or in pairs, moving quietly beneath forest vegetation. Fruit-bearing trees, undisturbed litter, and moist shaded ground can provide important feeding opportunities.
value.behavior: This is a secretive, ground-oriented dove that commonly walks or runs away when disturbed rather than flying immediately. If flushed, it usually makes a short, direct flight into nearby vegetation. Its plumage blends well with shadowed leaf litter and reddish-brown forest debris. The species is most active in quiet forest understory and may be easier to detect by its low, prolonged cooing calls than by sight.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. The species remains widespread, but local abundance can vary with the condition and continuity of forest habitat.
